name: secure-base-action
intent: Centralize the presentation tier's shared security handling in one base handler that every action extends, or that the front controller invokes, so that authentication, authorization, session validation, input verification and audit logging run uniformly before any business action and are implemented in exactly one place.
problem: Handler classes in a presentation tier - servlets, action classes, controllers, command endpoints - each repeat the same security work before their business logic: establish the caller's identity, check permission for this operation, validate the session, verify or canonicalize input, and record security-relevant events. The copies drift apart, the ordering differs between handlers, and a newly added action can silently omit a check. The recurring decision is where to put the shared security handling so that it is written once, ordered correctly, and impossible for an action to skip by accident.
context: Request handling in a layered enterprise application where a front controller or router dispatches to action objects or handler methods, where a session and security context already exist per request, and where most actions share the same security preconditions but depend on per-request identity and authorization data. The team controls the dispatch path and can make one base handler the only way in - typically an MVC framework with an action hierarchy, a filter/interceptor pipeline, or an equivalent middleware stack.
benefits: Security processing is written and reviewed once: every action inherits the same authenticate, authorize, validate-session, validate-input and log sequence instead of reimplementing it, so coverage grows with the action hierarchy rather than with reviewer diligence.

Enforcement order is fixed in one place - identity before authorization before session- or resource-dependent decisions - which removes the bug class where one action checks in a different order or skips a precondition.
Actions become business-only units: handler code reads as domain logic with no inline security, which makes both the action and the policy easier to reason about and to review.

One extension point for cross-cutting change: adding a check, reordering the steps, replacing the session validator or wiring a new audit sink is a change to the base, not a sweep across every action.
Failures get a uniform contract: the base translates a rejected request into one response shape (redirect, 401, 403, audit entry) instead of each action inventing its own.

The pattern names its collaborators explicitly (authentication enforcer, authorization enforcer, secure session manager, intercepting validator, secure logger), so the base delegates to dedicated components instead of accumulating mechanisms.
tradeoffs: Inheritance coupling: every action depends on the base's collaborators and lifecycle, so a change to the base potentially affects the whole presentation tier, and a single action cannot be tested without the base's context or a substitute.

Coverage is load-bearing: the guarantee holds only for requests that reach an action through the base. Direct servlet or endpoint access, batch jobs, internal calls and new transports bypass it silently, so coverage must be asserted rather than assumed.

Base-class bloat: the base is the natural home for every cross-cutting concern, and without discipline it accretes logging, error shaping, transactions and caching until it becomes a god object that is risky to change and hard to test.

Implicit, order-dependent semantics: the security sequence lives in the base's execution order, so overriding a hook or inserting a step in the wrong place can weaken policy without a compiler or a test noticing.

Static policy shape: a check-then-run base fits coarse rules applied uniformly; per-operation, data-dependent or tenant-dependent policies need metadata and overrides, and slowly leak decision logic back into the actions.

Framework friction: where the platform already intercepts compositionally (servlet filters, action filters, middleware, AOP), an inheritance-based base duplicates that pipeline, and in non-OO stacks the structure must be rebuilt with wrappers or dispatch tables.
Per-request state hazard: identity, session or audit context cached on the base instance or in thread-locals must be cleared between requests, or it leaks across users and requests.

participants.responsibility: Abstract base handler that every presentation action extends, or that the front controller invokes; owns the fixed security sequence (authenticate, authorize, validate session, validate input, audit) and runs it before deferring to the concrete action's business step. It is the only place the checks are wired.
Implements one business operation and contains no security code; it only ever receives requests that already passed the base's checks.
Determines which action handles a request and invokes it through the base handler, so that every routed request crosses the security sequence; the base's guarantee depends on this single entry point.
Establishes or verifies the caller's identity and makes the authenticated subject available to the later steps.
Decides whether the authenticated subject may perform this action, typically against operation-level rules; runs after authentication.
Validates and, where needed, refreshes or invalidates the session before the action relies on it.
Rejects malformed or out-of-policy request data before it reaches the business action.
Records security-relevant events, both granted and denied, without leaking credentials or personal data; invoked by the base for every outcome.
Carries the subject, session and request-scoped security state through the pipeline; populated by the authentication step and consumed by authorization, audit and the action.

use_cases: A Servlet/JSP or Struts-style web application in which every action class extends one secure base action that enforces login, role checks, session validity and input validation before the action's execute method runs.
An ASP.NET Core MVC application with a shared base controller or global authorization filter that runs the same authorization, session and audit steps for every controller action.
A Django or Rails application whose project base view or base controller composes the framework's authentication and permission checks, so individual views state only their business behaviour.
A multi-tenant SaaS backend where every inbound operation must resolve the tenant, verify the caller's membership of it and stamp an audit record before the handler executes.
An internal admin application where all privileged operations must be restricted to a role and logged, with one choke point that a security review can audit.
A migration from scattered inline checks to one policy path, where existing actions are rebased onto a single handler as the first step of centralizing security processing.

Apache Struts 2 applications built on the framework's base action (ActionSupport), where the default interceptor stack - validation, type conversion, double-submit protection - runs before every Action and can stop its execution, the framework's realization of the pattern's base-plus-pipeline security sequence.

A Ruby on Rails application that places before_action :authenticate_user! (typically the Devise helper) in ApplicationController so every inherited controller halts unauthenticated requests with one redirect contract before any action body runs.

A Django project whose class-based views mix in AccessMixin subclasses (LoginRequiredMixin, PermissionRequiredMixin), which override dispatch() to run authentication and permission checks ahead of the handler and funnel every denial through a single handle_no_permission() response.
avoid_when: The request path already has a compositional interception point - servlet filters, middleware, action filters, AOP interceptors - used consistently: extending that pipeline is simpler and less coupled than introducing an inheritance-based base handler.
There are only a handful of endpoints: plain guard clauses or decorators at each entry point are cheaper and clearer than a hierarchy with security hook semantics.
The policy is per-operation, data-dependent or delegated to an external decision point: a policy-enforcement pipeline carries that variation better than a base class's fixed sequence.
The language or framework has no action hierarchy and no dominant server framework: a middleware or dispatch-table wrapper is the honest realization, not a hand-rolled base class.
Actions are reachable from several entry points or are invoked internally: if the dispatch path cannot be funnelled, the base cannot guarantee coverage and the guarantee must be enforced elsewhere.
anti_patterns: Optional base action: the base exists but extending it is a convention rather than the only way in, so new actions quietly skip it and the shared checks cover only part of the surface.

God base action: authentication, authorization, session handling, validation, logging, transactions, caching and error rendering accumulate in one class until it is untestable and changes are avoided instead of made.

Base action as the only defence: once the base checks exist, alternate entry points - admin endpoints, batch imports, direct service calls, debug routes - are left unguarded because 'the base handles security'.
Policy in the base, mechanism in the actions: role tables and resource comparisons are hard-coded in the base instead of delegated to enforcer components, so every policy change edits shared code.
Overridable checks: the base exposes its security steps as unprotected virtual or public methods, and subclasses override them to skip or weaken checks for convenience.
Order by accident: the step sequence is undocumented and unpinned by tests, so a refactor silently reorders authentication and authorization or drops a step for some actions.
design_principles: Single point of definition (DRY): shared security handling is expressed once, in the base handler, and inherited or consumed by every action.
Separation of concerns: actions own business logic, the base owns the security sequence, and the enforcer components own individual security mechanisms.
Template method / Hollywood principle: the base defines the request skeleton and calls the action's business step, so control stays with the security logic.
Complete mediation: every action invocation passes through the same decision path - a property to be asserted, since bypass is the pattern's main failure mode.
Fail-safe defaults: when a check cannot run - missing context, failed collaborator - the base aborts the request rather than continuing to the action.
Least knowledge: the action sees only validated, authorized requests and stays unaware of how the checks were performed.
best_practices: Make the base the only way in: route every presentation action through one dispatcher or base handler, and test or lint for coverage so a new endpoint cannot bypass it unnoticed.
Keep the base thin and delegate: it composes the enforcers (authentication, authorization, session, validation, audit) and contains sequencing and failure translation, not policy logic.

Pin the order in tests: assert that authentication precedes authorization, that session validation precedes resource-dependent checks, and that any failure short-circuits before the action is invoked.
Fail closed: if a collaborator is missing, misconfigured or throws, reject the request and record why; never continue to the business action on an error path.
Keep the business step abstract and the hook set minimal: a final template method plus a few documented extension points beats a base full of overridable security methods.
Clear request-scoped state explicitly: identity, session and audit context must be reset between requests, especially in pooled, threaded or thread-local environments.
Design the audit trail with the base: record every decision, granted and denied, with actor, operation and outcome, without logging credentials or personal data.
sources: Steel, Nagappan & Lai, Core Security Patterns: Best Practices and Strategies for J2EE, Web Services, and Identity Management, Prentice Hall (2005) - the Secure Base Action pattern in Chapter 9, Securing the Web Tier, where it centralizes presentation-tier security and coordinates the Authentication Enforcer, Authorization Enforcer, Secure Session Manager, Intercepting Validator and Secure Logger.

https://web.archive.org/web/20191115131441id_/http://coresecuritypatterns.websecuritypatterns.com/patterns.htm - catalog entry: the secure base action centralizes and coordinates security-related tasks in the presentation tier, serves as the primary entry point, and should be extended or used by a front controller.

https://web.archive.org/web/20200131195209id_/http://coresecuritypatterns.websecuritypatterns.com/downloads/TOC.pdf - table of contents confirming Secure Base Action in Chapter 9, Securing the Web Tier.

https://cm.tm.kit.edu/download/Authentication_and_Authorization_Patterns_in_Spring_Security.pdf - mapping of the Core Security Patterns web-tier patterns onto the Spring Security filter chain, the framework realization used by the Java language file.

https://struts.apache.org/core-developers/interceptors - Apache Struts 2 official documentation: interceptors run before and after every Action and can prevent its execution (validation, double-submit protection), the framework pipeline wrapped around the base action class that realizes the pattern's security sequence.

https://guides.rubyonrails.org/action_controller_overview.html - Ruby on Rails official guide: a before_action placed in ApplicationController runs for every controller and halts the request cycle (e.g. redirect to login) before the action; documents skip_before_action, the built-in per-action opt-out that erodes complete mediation if used carelessly.

https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.0/topics/auth/default/ - Django official documentation: AccessMixin, LoginRequiredMixin and PermissionRequiredMixin override dispatch() to run authentication and permission checks before the view handler and route denials through one handle_no_permission() response path.

https://productsecurity.ghost.io/inheritance-based-auth-where-it-breaks/ - misuse analysis: inheritance-based authentication/authorization implemented in a base controller is effective but insufficient at scale, because bypass paths - controllers outside the hierarchy, alternate entry points, opted-out actions - create coverage gaps exactly where the base's guarantee silently lapses.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fragile_base_class_problem - the fragile base class problem: changes to a base class can unintentionally break derived classes that depend on its implementation details, the classic criticism of shipping shared behavior (here, the security sequence) through inheritance.
